scope.purpose: Preserve collaboratively agreed project-authored concepts and blocked boundaries without opening any evidence approval gate.

agreed_project_authored_concepts.wording: Electrical-insulating glove selection must be based on maximum system voltage, applicable safety requirements, glove rating, inspection status, and the vehicle-specific service procedure.
Use cable markings, routing, connectors, system documentation, and applicable vehicle-specific service information to identify high-voltage conductors; do not rely on color alone.

Body position and minimizing possible current paths can reduce exposure risk, but these practices do not replace de-energization, isolation, verification of absence of voltage, appropriate PPE, rated test equipment, and vehicle-specific service procedures.

Test equipment can create an unintended current path when its reference or ground connection is not electrically isolated from earth ground; isolation characteristics, voltage rating, measurement category, probe configuration, and vehicle-specific procedure must be verified before connection.
A digital multimeter must be selected for the expected voltage, measurement category, transient exposure, lead and probe rating, and test environment.
Teach the purpose and limitations of insulation-resistance testing while keeping test voltage, connection points, component isolation, and acceptance criteria vehicle- or component-specific.
Use applicable vehicle-specific service information to identify a high-voltage service disconnect or isolation point, required access conditions, and the approved disable and enable procedure.
Electrical-insulating gloves must be correctly rated, inspected, maintained, stored, and used according to applicable safety requirements and manufacturer instructions.
A DC-DC converter transfers electrical energy between DC voltage domains by changing voltage level as required by the vehicle architecture.
Step-down conversion reduces a DC voltage level and step-up conversion raises it; actual vehicle modules may combine these functions or use other topologies.

Compare how a DC-DC converter supports low-voltage systems in electrified vehicles with conventional low-voltage supply architectures without assuming the same components are replaced on every vehicle.
Explain switching devices, energy-storage elements, rectification or synchronous switching, and filtering conceptually; exact topology and switching strategy remain design-specific.
Identify converter hazards and use vehicle-specific service information to determine required isolation, PPE, equipment ratings, verification steps, and access restrictions.
Use the applicable wiring diagram or schematic to identify the low-voltage output circuit, including relevant power paths, grounds, protection devices, connectors, and connected loads.
Use vehicle-specific service information to locate approved test points and expected operating range before measuring converter low-voltage output.

A vehicle power inverter converts electrical energy between DC and AC forms as required by the propulsion system while controlling electrical characteristics delivered to or received from an electric machine.
Power-electronic switching devices are controlled in timed patterns to regulate energy flow and produce required electrical waveforms; PWM is one common control method.
The inverter regulates electrical parameters such as voltage, current, frequency, and phase according to the propulsion system control strategy, influencing motor torque, speed, and direction.
Some electrified-vehicle power-electronics systems use boost conversion to raise DC bus voltage above source voltage; presence, topology, and control strategy are architecture-specific.
During regenerative braking, the electric machine can operate as a generator and return electrical energy through the power-electronics system toward the energy-storage system under vehicle control.

Power-electronics and battery systems require thermal management; cooling and heating methods depend on vehicle design and may use air, liquid, refrigerant-assisted, electrical heating, or combined strategies.
Temperature data can influence power output, cooling operation, charging, propulsion behavior, derating, or protective shutdown strategies, with thresholds remaining system-specific.
An electrified vehicle can use a DC-DC converter to support the low-voltage bus and maintain the auxiliary battery subject to operating state and control strategy.
Compare measured voltage and current behavior with vehicle-specific documented expectations while considering auxiliary-battery condition, converter command state, electrical load, and system faults.

High-voltage systems are designed to maintain electrical isolation from the vehicle chassis, and isolation faults must be diagnosed using vehicle-specific information, approved equipment, and documented procedures.

A weak or unstable low-voltage supply can contribute to abnormal wake-up behavior, communication faults, contactor-control problems, misleading symptoms, or failure to enter the expected operating state.
High-voltage systems may use controlled precharge to limit inrush current before main contactors fully connect the high-voltage source to the DC bus; sequence and limits are vehicle-specific.

Battery-management systems monitor pack and, where applicable, module or cell-group voltages to evaluate operating condition, detect abnormal imbalance, support state estimation, and protect the energy-storage system.

Vehicle energy-management systems coordinate propulsion demand, available battery power, charging opportunities, thermal conditions, and protection limits to determine how electrical energy is stored, converted, and used.

Combine fault codes, live data, voltage and temperature trends, operating conditions, system commands, and applicable service information; do not treat one measurement or fault code as sufficient evidence of battery failure.
State of charge and state of health are calculated or estimated system quantities derived from multiple inputs and operating history rather than direct measurements from a single voltage reading.
Evaluate cell or cell-group voltage differences in the context of architecture, operating state, temperature, and load instead of applying one universal allowable difference.

Reduced usable capacity is evidence of degradation but should be evaluated with battery-management estimates, operating conditions, diagnostic data, and manufacturer criteria before determining failure.
Distinguish normal thermal-management activity, abnormal overheating, fault conditions, and confirmed thermal-runaway events using battery- and vehicle-specific information.
A battery-related diagnostic trouble code identifies a detected condition or diagnostic path, not necessarily the failed component.

A confirmed battery-related fault does not automatically justify complete pack replacement; repair level depends on battery design, evidence, manufacturer information, safety restrictions, authorization, and applicable warranty or recycling requirements.
Use labels, component identifiers, vehicle documentation, and manufacturer information to identify battery type, chemistry, configuration, and relevant service information.

Identification and specification data describe documented design information while live diagnostic data describe current measured or calculated operating condition; do not treat catalog or label specifications as live diagnostic evidence.
Distinguish commanded values, measured values, and calculated or estimated values when interpreting battery-system data.
Evaluate battery-system data over time and under known operating conditions because trends can reveal patterns that a single snapshot may not show.
Cross-check unusual values against related signals, operating conditions, and expected relationships before treating them as confirmed faults.
Diagnose related low-voltage, communication, thermal-management, charging, propulsion-control, and high-voltage faults together when evidence suggests a shared cause or dependency.

Capture fault codes, freeze-frame or event data, live parameters, operating conditions, battery state information, and related system status before clearing codes, disconnecting components, or performing resets.
Repeat relevant checks under applicable documented operating conditions and record before-and-after evidence to confirm that the original fault condition has been corrected.
Record the original concern, relevant evidence, tests performed, results obtained, alternative causes considered, basis for the repair decision, and evidence used to verify the result.
Classify conclusions as supported, not supported, or not yet determined when evidence is incomplete, unavailable, contradictory, or not comparable.

blocked_universalizations: cable color as sole high-voltage identification
one-hand rule as a substitute for isolation and verification
generic meter category or insulation-test procedure
fixed DC-DC, inverter, battery, thermal, or precharge values
universal SOC, SOH, imbalance, capacity, isolation, or replacement thresholds
manufacturer-specific algorithms or procedures presented as universal
diagnosis or replacement based on one DTC, one measurement, one snapshot, or one catalog value

rules: Catalog or label specifications are not converted into universal diagnostic thresholds.
Secondary educational material does not override vehicle-specific service information.
No attached reference is ingested, chunked, rights-cleared, technically approved, or lesson-mapped by this record.

diagnostic_principles: A single clue can justify another test; it does not automatically prove root cause.
Unsupported evidence remains unavailable, not comparable, or not yet determined rather than being inferred.
